reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: Produces a sedative-hypnotic toxidrome of drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia, and depressed consciousness, typically with preserved or only mildly depressed vital signs
Taken alone, benzodiazepines rarely cause death; serious respiratory depression usually reflects co-ingestion of alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, or the parenteral route
The mainstay of care is supportive - airway protection, breathing support, and observation - rather than any specific antidote in most cases
Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that reverses sedation, but its use is limited because it can precipitate seizures and a withdrawal state, particularly in chronic users or mixed overdoses
Flumazenil is especially hazardous when a proconvulsant (such as a tricyclic antidepressant) has been co-ingested, as it removes the seizure threshold-raising effect of the benzodiazepine
Marked or fluctuating conscious level, disproportionate hypotension, or significant respiratory depression should prompt a search for a co-ingested agent
Activated charcoal offers little benefit and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient, so it is generally not recommended
Consider alternative causes of coma (hypoglycaemia, head injury, other intoxicants) if the clinical picture does not fit a pure benzodiazepine effect
reference.pathophysiology: Benzodiazepines enhance the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, producing central nervous system depression. Because they modulate rather than directly open the channel, there is a ceiling to their respiratory depressant effect when taken alone, which explains their relatively wide margin of safety in isolated overdose. When combined with other central depressants such as opioids or alcohol, this ceiling is lost and dangerous synergistic respiratory depression can occur.
additionalDifferentials: Structural or metabolic causes of coma
Carbon monoxide or other toxic causes of reduced consciousness
additionalInvestigations: Capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Pulse oximetry and, if indicated, arterial blood gas for hypoventilation
Paracetamol and salicylate levels and an ECG to screen for co-ingestants
Urine or serum toxicology where it will change management
CT head if reduced consciousness is unexplained or focal signs are present
redFlags: Deep or fluctuating coma suggesting a co-ingested agent
Hypotension out of proportion to isolated benzodiazepine effect
Loss of airway protective reflexes with aspiration risk
Seizures, which should raise concern for a proconvulsant co-ingestant rather than benzodiazepine alone
reference.prognosis: Isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually has an excellent prognosis with supportive care, but outcome worsens considerably with co-ingestion of other central depressants or when aspiration or prolonged hypoxia occurs.
pitfalls: Reflexively giving flumazenil and precipitating seizures or acute withdrawal, especially in chronic users or mixed overdose
Attributing deep coma or hypotension to benzodiazepines alone and missing a co-ingestant
Overlooking hypoglycaemia or another treatable cause of reduced consciousness
Administering charcoal to a drowsy patient and causing aspiration
management: Prioritise supportive care with airway protection, breathing support and observation, which is the mainstay for isolated ingestion
Reserve flumazenil for carefully selected cases, avoiding it in chronic users or suspected proconvulsant co-ingestion because it can precipitate seizures and a withdrawal state
Search actively for co-ingested central depressants such as opioids or alcohol when consciousness is disproportionately or fluctuatingly depressed
Screen with capillary glucose, paracetamol and salicylate levels and an ECG for co-ingestants
Monitor conscious level, oxygenation and ventilation, escalating to airway support for significant respiratory depression or aspiration risk
Provide psychiatric assessment and follow-up after recovery where the overdose was intentional
